transcript.content: Hello, welcome. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Yeah, so, I guess I'm here because... well, it's been a really long time coming, honestly. I've been trying to just deal with it on my own for months now, because I figured I just needed more discipline or something, right? But I'm in this radiologic tech program right now, taking college classes and doing clinicals, and it's just becoming completely impossible. 

Like, when I'm in the radiology suite waiting on the imaging equipment, or especially when I'm stuck in a lecture hall for these long, dragged-out anatomy classes, I'm supposed to just sit there and be still. But I literally feel like I'm crawling out of my skin. It's this crazy, intense physical feeling, like this pressure building up in my legs and my chest, and I just can't take it. I try to tough it out, I really do, for months I've been trying to just force myself to stay in the chair and act normal, but I always end up constantly shifting around, readjusting, bouncing my leg until the whole row of desks is shaking, or I just have to get up. 

I'll find literally any excuse to move—like, I'll pretend I need to go organize the lead aprons in the supply closet, or I'll go to the bathroom three times during a lecture just so I can pace the hallways for a minute. I just end up pacing and moving constantly because sitting still is just... it's unbearable, and my instructors are definitely starting to look at me funny, so I figured I really needed to come in and talk to someone about it.
Do you find yourself feeling this restless and unable to sit still in other situations, like when you're at home watching TV, in a car, or during social gatherings?

You know, I'm... I'm not really sure? I haven't actually noticed it as much in those kinds of situations, to be perfectly honest. Like, take watching TV at home, for instance. I don't really ever just sit down on the couch and stare at the screen anyway. If the TV is on, it's usually just background noise while I'm doing something else, like maybe I'm wandering around the kitchen making a sandwich, or I'm standing up messing with my phone, or I'm reorganizing my backpack for clinicals the next day. So I'm already moving, you know? I don't get that horrible trapped feeling because nobody is forcing me to stay on the couch. 

And as for being in the car... well, I actually drive a manual transmission, which I specifically bought because I like having both my hands and my feet busy. Working the clutch, shifting gears, checking the mirrors—it keeps me occupied, so I don't really feel that same intense pressure building up in my chest when I'm driving. 

And with social stuff, like if I'm at a buddy's house or a party or whatever, it's totally different than a lecture hall. If you're hanging out with friends, nobody cares if you get up and pace around the backyard, or if you stand by the snack table the whole time instead of sitting in a chair. It's just not like anatomy class where Dr. Davis—he's my professor, super strict guy, always peering over his glasses at everyone—where he literally glares at you if your chair even squeaks. So, yeah, I guess I just haven't really paid attention to it outside of school and the hospital, mostly because I'm not being forced to stay glued to one spot in those other places, if that makes sense?
Do you ever feel restless or have trouble staying still when you're by yourself and not in class or clinicals—like if you're trying to relax, read a book, or just sit quietly for a few minutes?

Well, see, that's the thing about trying to relax or do something quiet... it never really stays quiet for very long. Like, even if I'm doing something I genuinely enjoy, something I really want to be doing, I just can't keep still or keep quiet. 

For example, I really like editing photos—I do some photography on the side, mostly just for fun, you know, taking my camera out hiking or whatever—and sometimes I like to sketch, too. But even when I'm sitting down at my desk, trying to focus on adjusting the contrast on a photo or getting a sketch just right, I can't just sit there in silence. It's like my body refuses to let the room be quiet. I'll start tapping my pen on the desk, or drumming my fingers on the edge of the keyboard, or I'll just start humming some random song that's been stuck in my head all day. 

And if there's anyone else around, like my roommates or the guys in the computer lab on campus, I'm constantly talking to them. I'll just start making comments about whatever I'm doing, or asking them questions, or just thinking out loud, you know? And I end up getting up from my chair a million times, too. Like, I'll edit one photo, and then I have to stand up and stretch, or go get a glass of water, or pace around the room for a second before I can sit back down and look at the next one. 

It gets to the point where the guys at the lab or my roommates are always telling me to settle down or keep it down because I'm making too much noise or moving around too much. They're always like, "Dude, can you just sit still for five minutes?" or "Do you have to tap on everything?" And I don't even realize I'm doing half of it until they point it out! It's just... it's like I have to be making some kind of noise or movement, even when I'm supposedly relaxing or doing something low-key by myself.

When you're completely alone and there's no one around to interact with—like late at night in your room or when you're waiting by yourself—do you still feel restless or have a hard time just sitting quietly without needing to move or make noise?

Well, yeah, honestly, even when I'm totally alone, it's pretty much the same deal. Like, say it's 2 AM and I'm just in my room, trying to wind down or whatever. You'd think I could just sit there and chill, right? But no, it's like my brain and my body just won't get on the same page. I'll be sitting on my bed, maybe trying to read an article for class or just scrolling on my phone, and I'll still be bouncing my leg. Or I'll start clicking my tongue, or humming, or just talking to myself. I actually talk to myself a lot when I'm alone. I'll just be narrating what I'm doing, like, "Okay, let's go check the fridge," or "Man, I really need to finish this assignment." 

And waiting? Oh man, waiting by myself is the absolute worst. Like, if I'm at the laundromat late at night—because sometimes I do my laundry super late to avoid the crowds—and I'm just sitting there waiting for the dryer to finish. It's only, what, 40 minutes? But to me, it feels like an eternity. I can't just sit in the plastic chairs and stare at the wall or look at my phone the whole time. I'll get up, pace the aisles between the machines, read the bulletin board with all those old, faded flyers for guitar lessons and lost cats, maybe go outside and walk a lap around the building, come back in, sit down for two minutes, and then I'm back up again. 

I just... I don't know, I just don't have an "off" switch, I guess. Even when there's literally no one around to bother and no reason I can't just sit in silence, the silence itself just feels wrong. It feels too heavy or something. So I end up filling it with movement or noise, even if it's just me tapping my foot against the side of the bed or drumming my fingers on the steering wheel while I'm waiting in a drive-thru line by myself. It's like I have this motor inside me that's just constantly idling too high, and I have to let some of that energy out somehow, even when I'm completely alone in the middle of the night.
Do you find it hard to focus or concentrate on tasks, even ones you're interested in, or do you often lose track of what you're doing?

Focus? Um... no, not really. I mean, I don't think so? I don't really have a problem paying attention or anything like that. Like, if I'm doing something, I'm totally dialed into it. 

Take my clinicals at the hospital, right? We have to learn all these super specific positioning techniques for different exams—like, say you're doing a routine hand series, you have to get the PA, the oblique, the lateral, and you have to make sure the X-ray beam is centered exactly over the third metacarpophalangeal joint, and you have to adjust the light field just right so you're not radiating unnecessary tissue. I can remember all of that perfectly. I don't lose track of the steps or forget what I'm doing halfway through positioning the patient. I'm completely focused on getting the image right. It's just that, you know, while I'm doing it, I might be bouncing on my heels, or talking the patient's ear off about the weather, or drumming my fingers on the control panel behind the lead glass. But my brain is one hundred percent on the task. 

Same thing with my photography or photo editing. I can zero in on a picture for a really long time. I know exactly what I want to do with the contrast or the shadows, and I don't just space out or forget what my goal was. I'm just physically moving the whole time I'm doing it. Like I was saying before with the pen tapping and the humming—I'm doing all that extra stuff, but I'm still totally focused on the screen. It's not like my mind is wandering off into the clouds. I don't really daydream at all, actually. 

Even in lectures, like with Dr. Davis, I hear every single word he's saying about bone pathology or whatever. I'm absorbing the information, I'm taking the notes, I'm just... I just happen to be shifting in my seat and shaking my leg so hard the desk vibrates while I'm listening. So, yeah, I wouldn't say I lose track of things or can't concentrate. My brain is always going, but it's usually going exactly where I want it to, if that makes sense. It's just my body that won't cooperate.
Do you ever feel nervous, anxious, or worried, especially in situations where you're not being asked to sit still or focus on a task?

Nervous? Anxious? No, man, not at all. That's actually something people get wrong about me a lot, honestly. Because I'm always moving, you know, always bouncing around or tapping my foot or pacing, people look at me and go, "Whoa, what are you so stressed out about?" or "Why are you so nervous?" But I'm really not! Mentally, I'm actually a super chill guy. I don't sit around worrying about things or overthinking stuff at all. 

Take the ER, for instance. We rotate through the emergency department for our clinicals, right? And sometimes it gets totally insane down there. Like, a trauma code will come in over the radio—maybe a bad car wreck out on the interstate or something—and suddenly everyone is rushing around, the nurses are yelling, the trauma docs are prepping the bay, and we have to be ready with the portable X-ray machine the second they need a chest or pelvis film. A lot of the other students in my cohort get super freaked out. They get all sweaty and anxious, like, "Oh man, what if I mess up the technique, what if I get in the surgeon's way?" But me? I love it. I'm not anxious at all. I'm just pumped up. I'm bouncing on my toes, totally ready to go, just waiting for them to yell "clear" so I can shoot the image. 

Or even just in regular, everyday stuff where there's no pressure to sit still or do a job. Like if I'm just hanging out at a buddy's apartment on a Friday night, playing video games or whatever. I'm not sitting there stressing about my grades or worrying about some awkward thing I said three years ago. My brain just doesn't do that anxiety loop thing that some people talk about. I'm just... energetic, you know? Like, I might be standing up behind the couch while we're playing Smash Bros instead of sitting on it, and I might be talking a mile a minute, but it's not from nerves. My mom used to do that all the time when I was a kid, she'd see me pacing before we'd go somewhere and ask, "Are you worried about going to the party?" and I'd have to tell her, no, I'm just excited, I just want to go! 

So yeah, I don't really get worried or anxious like that. It's strictly a physical energy thing, just this constant need to be doing something, but it's definitely not a nervous mental thing. I'm actually pretty relaxed in my head, even if my body is doing a marathon.
Have you ever had periods where you felt down, hopeless, or lost interest in things you usually enjoy, even when things aren’t stressful or demanding?

Down or hopeless? Um... no. No, I really don't think so. I mean, I hear people talk about that, like getting in a funk where they just want to lay in bed all day and not do anything, but I honestly can't even imagine that. Like, my brain just doesn't go there. If I'm awake, I'm ready to do something. 

I've never had a time where I just lost interest in the stuff I like. Take my photography—I think I mentioned I do photo editing earlier? Man, I could do that for hours, every single day, and I never get bored or feel like I don't want to do it. Even if nothing stressful is going on, or even if I *am* stressed, I still want to do my hobbies. Like last month, we had midterms in my rad tech program, and it was a ton of studying, especially for radiation physics, which is just... man, it's a lot of formulas. Inverse square law and all that. And some of the guys in my study group were getting super burnt out and down about it, just totally over it and not wanting to hang out or play Xbox or anything. But me? I was still totally down for whatever. I'd finish a three-hour study session and be bouncing on my heels like, "Alright, who wants to go play basketball?" or "Let's go drive somewhere and get food." 

I just don't lose my spark for things. I'm pretty much always upbeat. My mom actually used to say I was born with a smile on my face because I just never really get sad or mopey. I mean, sure, if a movie is sad or I fail a quiz I might be bummed for like, ten minutes, but a whole period of feeling hopeless? Or just losing interest in my life for no reason? Nah, definitely not me. I just have way too much stuff I want to do, you know? There's always a new technique to learn or a new place I want to go take pictures of, so I never really hit that wall where I feel empty or lost.
Looking back, were you always this energetic and restless, even when you were younger—like back in elementary school or middle school?

Oh, man, always. Yeah, one hundred percent always. It's funny you ask that, because some people think maybe it's just because my clinicals are so fast-paced now, or because college is a lot to handle, but no, this is just... it's just me. It's always been me. My parents actually still talk about it, like they'll bring it up at family dinners just to tease me. They talk about these parent-teacher conferences from back in elementary school—like, way back, first or second grade. 

The teachers were always telling my parents how I was just constantly out of my seat. I could never just sit at my little desk like the other kids. I'd be up walking to the trash can, or going to look out the window, or just standing up right next to my chair while I was supposed to be doing a worksheet. And the teachers said I was always calling out, too. Like, they would ask the class a math question or something, and I wouldn't even bother raising my hand, I'd just blurt the answer out right over everyone else because I just couldn't hold it in and wait my turn. 

I was also always rushing ahead before the directions were even finished. The teacher would be standing at the front of the room explaining how to do an assignment, and I'd already be halfway done with the page before she even got to step two. I just had to go, go, go, you know? I just wanted to get to the action part. So, yeah, that was all happening way, way before middle school even started. It's definitely not just something that popped up recently since I started my radiology training. It's literally been my whole life, just this constant motor running since I was in Velcro shoes.
As a child, did you often act without thinking, like interrupting others, blurting out answers, or doing things without considering the consequences?

Oh, man, definitely. Like I was just saying about the math questions in first grade, that was my whole childhood. I'd just spit the answer out before anyone else could even process what the teacher was saying. But honestly, it's not even just a back-then thing. It’s still happening to me right now, and it actually gets me into some pretty awkward spots at the hospital. 

Like, during my clinicals, we have to learn all these super specific angles and setups, right? And when a supervisor is explaining a positioning step to me—you know, like how to angle the tube for a specific shoulder view or a sunrise patella—or if they start asking me a question to test my knowledge, I just... I jump right in with the answer before they even finish talking. My brain just hears the first few words and goes, 'Oh, I know this one!' so I just blurt it right out. 

But then, almost immediately, I realize I completely missed the part that actually mattered. Like, they were about to tell me a crucial modification because the patient has a fractured collarbone or can't stand up straight, and because I cut them off to show I knew the basic setup, I totally missed the important detail. It happens all the time. I'm not trying to be disrespectful or act like a know-it-all, I swear I'm not. My mouth just kind of fires off before I can hit the brakes. And then I have to stand there and awkwardly ask them to repeat the second half of their sentence, which makes the techs look at me like I'm not paying attention. But I am paying attention! I'm just paying attention too fast, if that makes sense? Like, just the other week, we had this portable chest X-ray in the ICU, and the lead tech was trying to tell me about the patient's chest tube, and I just jumped right in talking about the grid alignment, and... yeah. It's a whole thing. I just act first and think about it like two seconds too late.

doctor.question: Do you find it hard to focus or concentrate on tasks, even ones you're interested in, or do you often lose track of what you're doing?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty focusing or concentrating on tasks, which relates to inattention symptoms. My symptom profile only includes hyperactive/impulsive symptoms (restlessness, difficulty engaging in quiet activities, constant activity, blurting answers, difficulty waiting turn), so I do not have a symptom for poor focus or concentration.

patient.answer:
Focus? Um... no, not really. I mean, I don't think so? I don't really have a problem paying attention or anything like that. Like, if I'm doing something, I'm totally dialed into it. 

Take my clinicals at the hospital, right? We have to learn all these super specific positioning techniques for different exams—like, say you're doing a routine hand series, you have to get the PA, the oblique, the lateral, and you have to make sure the X-ray beam is centered exactly over the third metacarpophalangeal joint, and you have to adjust the light field just right so you're not radiating unnecessary tissue. I can remember all of that perfectly. I don't lose track of the steps or forget what I'm doing halfway through positioning the patient. I'm completely focused on getting the image right. It's just that, you know, while I'm doing it, I might be bouncing on my heels, or talking the patient's ear off about the weather, or drumming my fingers on the control panel behind the lead glass. But my brain is one hundred percent on the task. 

Same thing with my photography or photo editing. I can zero in on a picture for a really long time. I know exactly what I want to do with the contrast or the shadows, and I don't just space out or forget what my goal was. I'm just physically moving the whole time I'm doing it. Like I was saying before with the pen tapping and the humming—I'm doing all that extra stuff, but I'm still totally focused on the screen. It's not like my mind is wandering off into the clouds. I don't really daydream at all, actually. 

Even in lectures, like with Dr. Davis, I hear every single word he's saying about bone pathology or whatever. I'm absorbing the information, I'm taking the notes, I'm just... I just happen to be shifting in my seat and shaking my leg so hard the desk vibrates while I'm listening. So, yeah, I wouldn't say I lose track of things or can't concentrate. My brain is always going, but it's usually going exactly where I want it to, if that makes sense. It's just my body that won't cooperate.

inference.note: The patient reports significant restlessness and inability to remain still in structured, stationary settings (e.g., lectures, waiting), with associated motor overactivity even when alone. However, concentration and focus on tasks—especially those of interest—are preserved. This supports consideration of F90.0 (ADHD, predominantly hyperactive/impulsive presentation) rather than attentional deficits alone. F43.13 (Adjustment Disorder with Mixed Anxiety and Depressed Mood) remains due to the stress-related onset of symptoms in academic and clinical settings, though anxiety or depression are not the primary complaints. No definitive exclusion of either diagnosis at this time.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of anxiety that are separate from restlessness or hyperactivity, which could support a diagnosis of F43.13 (Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety) rather than F90.0 (ADHD, Predominantly Hyperactive-Impulsive Type).
doctor.question: Do you ever feel nervous, anxious, or worried, especially in situations where you're not being asked to sit still or focus on a task?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of anxiety, nervousness, or worry, which are not covered by my symptom profile of ADHD (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation).

patient.answer:
Nervous? Anxious? No, man, not at all. That's actually something people get wrong about me a lot, honestly. Because I'm always moving, you know, always bouncing around or tapping my foot or pacing, people look at me and go, "Whoa, what are you so stressed out about?" or "Why are you so nervous?" But I'm really not! Mentally, I'm actually a super chill guy. I don't sit around worrying about things or overthinking stuff at all. 

Take the ER, for instance. We rotate through the emergency department for our clinicals, right? And sometimes it gets totally insane down there. Like, a trauma code will come in over the radio—maybe a bad car wreck out on the interstate or something—and suddenly everyone is rushing around, the nurses are yelling, the trauma docs are prepping the bay, and we have to be ready with the portable X-ray machine the second they need a chest or pelvis film. A lot of the other students in my cohort get super freaked out. They get all sweaty and anxious, like, "Oh man, what if I mess up the technique, what if I get in the surgeon's way?" But me? I love it. I'm not anxious at all. I'm just pumped up. I'm bouncing on my toes, totally ready to go, just waiting for them to yell "clear" so I can shoot the image. 

Or even just in regular, everyday stuff where there's no pressure to sit still or do a job. Like if I'm just hanging out at a buddy's apartment on a Friday night, playing video games or whatever. I'm not sitting there stressing about my grades or worrying about some awkward thing I said three years ago. My brain just doesn't do that anxiety loop thing that some people talk about. I'm just... energetic, you know? Like, I might be standing up behind the couch while we're playing Smash Bros instead of sitting on it, and I might be talking a mile a minute, but it's not from nerves. My mom used to do that all the time when I was a kid, she'd see me pacing before we'd go somewhere and ask, "Are you worried about going to the party?" and I'd have to tell her, no, I'm just excited, I just want to go! 

So yeah, I don't really get worried or anxious like that. It's strictly a physical energy thing, just this constant need to be doing something, but it's definitely not a nervous mental thing. I'm actually pretty relaxed in my head, even if my body is doing a marathon.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of depression, specifically low mood, anhedonia, or feelings of worthlessness, which could indicate major depressive disorder (F43.13) as a comorbid condition.
doctor.question: Have you ever had periods where you felt down, hopeless, or lost interest in things you usually enjoy, even when things aren’t stressful or demanding?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of depression (feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in activities), which are not part of my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Down or hopeless? Um... no. No, I really don't think so. I mean, I hear people talk about that, like getting in a funk where they just want to lay in bed all day and not do anything, but I honestly can't even imagine that. Like, my brain just doesn't go there. If I'm awake, I'm ready to do something. 

I've never had a time where I just lost interest in the stuff I like. Take my photography—I think I mentioned I do photo editing earlier? Man, I could do that for hours, every single day, and I never get bored or feel like I don't want to do it. Even if nothing stressful is going on, or even if I *am* stressed, I still want to do my hobbies. Like last month, we had midterms in my rad tech program, and it was a ton of studying, especially for radiation physics, which is just... man, it's a lot of formulas. Inverse square law and all that. And some of the guys in my study group were getting super burnt out and down about it, just totally over it and not wanting to hang out or play Xbox or anything. But me? I was still totally down for whatever. I'd finish a three-hour study session and be bouncing on my heels like, "Alright, who wants to go play basketball?" or "Let's go drive somewhere and get food." 

I just don't lose my spark for things. I'm pretty much always upbeat. My mom actually used to say I was born with a smile on my face because I just never really get sad or mopey. I mean, sure, if a movie is sad or I fail a quiz I might be bummed for like, ten minutes, but a whole period of feeling hopeless? Or just losing interest in my life for no reason? Nah, definitely not me. I just have way too much stuff I want to do, you know? There's always a new technique to learn or a new place I want to go take pictures of, so I never really hit that wall where I feel empty or lost.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a history of symptoms before age 12, which is a diagnostic criterion for ADHD (F90.0).
doctor.question: Looking back, were you always this energetic and restless, even when you were younger—like back in elementary school or middle school?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: My parents still talk about elementary school conferences where teachers said I was always out of my seat, calling out, or rushing ahead before directions were finished. That was happening way before middle school, not just since radiology training.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if my symptoms of restlessness and high energy were present when I was younger, specifically in elementary or middle school, which corresponds to the requirement that symptoms were present prior to age 12.

patient.answer:
Oh, man, always. Yeah, one hundred percent always. It's funny you ask that, because some people think maybe it's just because my clinicals are so fast-paced now, or because college is a lot to handle, but no, this is just... it's just me. It's always been me. My parents actually still talk about it, like they'll bring it up at family dinners just to tease me. They talk about these parent-teacher conferences from back in elementary school—like, way back, first or second grade. 

The teachers were always telling my parents how I was just constantly out of my seat. I could never just sit at my little desk like the other kids. I'd be up walking to the trash can, or going to look out the window, or just standing up right next to my chair while I was supposed to be doing a worksheet. And the teachers said I was always calling out, too. Like, they would ask the class a math question or something, and I wouldn't even bother raising my hand, I'd just blurt the answer out right over everyone else because I just couldn't hold it in and wait my turn. 

I was also always rushing ahead before the directions were even finished. The teacher would be standing at the front of the room explaining how to do an assignment, and I'd already be halfway done with the page before she even got to step two. I just had to go, go, go, you know? I just wanted to get to the action part. So, yeah, that was all happening way, way before middle school even started. It's definitely not just something that popped up recently since I started my radiology training. It's literally been my whole life, just this constant motor running since I was in Velcro shoes.

target_item.name: Blurting_Answers

patient.answer:
Oh, man, definitely. Like I was just saying about the math questions in first grade, that was my whole childhood. I'd just spit the answer out before anyone else could even process what the teacher was saying. But honestly, it's not even just a back-then thing. It’s still happening to me right now, and it actually gets me into some pretty awkward spots at the hospital. 

Like, during my clinicals, we have to learn all these super specific angles and setups, right? And when a supervisor is explaining a positioning step to me—you know, like how to angle the tube for a specific shoulder view or a sunrise patella—or if they start asking me a question to test my knowledge, I just... I jump right in with the answer before they even finish talking. My brain just hears the first few words and goes, 'Oh, I know this one!' so I just blurt it right out. 

But then, almost immediately, I realize I completely missed the part that actually mattered. Like, they were about to tell me a crucial modification because the patient has a fractured collarbone or can't stand up straight, and because I cut them off to show I knew the basic setup, I totally missed the important detail. It happens all the time. I'm not trying to be disrespectful or act like a know-it-all, I swear I'm not. My mouth just kind of fires off before I can hit the brakes. And then I have to stand there and awkwardly ask them to repeat the second half of their sentence, which makes the techs look at me like I'm not paying attention. But I am paying attention! I'm just paying attention too fast, if that makes sense? Like, just the other week, we had this portable chest X-ray in the ICU, and the lead tech was trying to tell me about the patient's chest tube, and I just jumped right in talking about the grid alignment, and... yeah. It's a whole thing. I just act first and think about it like two seconds too late.
